I've been collecting and reading pretty rare or at least interesting books most would never see for awhile now and taking notes as I read. My goal was to start a blog, but I never get started.

I was encouraged by @doginventer to start putting drafts and notes on here so that I can get commentary and mold them into eventual worthwhile content. So I'm starting with an easy one which is basically just reporting what is in this book.

It's an academic text from 1966, edited by W. R. Derrick Sewell, with about 30 different academics submitting an article, basically describing the current state of affairs in weather modification and plans for the future. University of Chicago Press.

I'm just gonna do a run through, I do not take pride in this presentation, but any commentary will be useful as I'll try to make this interesting eventually instead of just a basic rundown.

The most important points is all that's here, they tend to cover the same points a lot from article to article.

Chapter 1 - Intro by Derrick Sewell

Sewell describes the current goal of climate modification which is basically improving economic productivity. This is the theme throughout the book with most chapters attempting to create models for effectiveely studying the effects of certain modifications.

The interesting points right off the start is that he describes weather modifcation as being everywhere and very active, "there are few parts of the U.S. where weather modification (WM) has not been undertaken" and "there have been at least 100 WM projects running since 1965." WM is apparently so widespread at this point (limited to rain and fog mostly) that there had been and were ongoing court cases between corporations trying to decide how to reimburse each other for profits and losses accrued from each other's modifications.

He ends with a general call for more study. Also he mentions that China, Russia, France, and a few others have active WM programs.

Chapter 2 - Gilbert White

He discusses the obvious complications of trying to manage the four main interlocking systems: Atmospheric, Hydrologic, Biologic, and Production & Communication. Following is a brief discussion on whether the main goal should be economic. He doesn't say it should be, but the rest of the entire book focuses on economic issues.

It becomes very clear the main goal of all these people is to increase productive capacity. Also he discusses that we need more study to understand what to reasonable expect as a return from our "investment." 1%, 10%? More?

Chatper 3 - P.H. Wycoff

Wycoff starts off discussing how it's been 20 years (!) since the Langmuir, Schaefer, and Vonnegut experiments of 1945-46 and we now understand that weather is much more complicated than we initially expected. He discusses the two main approaches to study; lab work and field testing. He concludes this work is too complicated to actually figure out in a lab and that field testing is necessary for proper advancement. He actually recommends combined approaches, but you can see he wants to just test in the field right off the jump.

Wycoff writes about proven things they can do, nothing special by today's standards like fog dissipation and increasing expected rainfall by 10-15% using silver iodide (SI) spraying as well as using sound and electricity to achieve the same thing, although the last two are cost prohibitive. (My side note, I think that's what they spray now and that HAARP plays in there somewhere.) There is a gym in this chapter where he discusses fog dissipation for landing planes during war. Apparently they had great success using massive heat around the runways. Obvoiusly that would work, but he writes "The pilots feel uneasy landing between walls of fire." LOL!

They can also suppress hail, blah blah. TNT, creating sonic booms is effective. They can reduce ground lightning strikes using SI seeding, etc. They can modify severe storms like hurricanes and reduce their wind speeds with SI seeding. He states, "The heat liberated by the freezing of the cold cloud droplets after massive quantities of SI are injected is approximately equivalent to the heat liberated by an atommic bomb, but acts over the period of many hours rather than minutes."

The Rest...

There are 27 more chapters with some good information but almost all of them focus on how to test the economic outcomes of more rainfall and how to credit and debit corporations (although they don't say "corporations") for their activity.

They study and attempt to measure runoff, transpiration, evaporation, humidity, evapotranspiration, etc. Stanford heavily involved and is running the first models by mid 50s.

Discussions on the law and policy ensue. Insurance, employment, investment, human behavior, animals, fish, etc. All speculation that really isn't that interesting. I barely trudge through it so I'm leaving it out now.

I hope this is interesting to someone. To me the interesting part is mainly hearing them openly and freely discuss an issue that has obviously been hushed up now. To me the idea that they stopped is ridiculous. Feel free to comment. I can give more detail on some things I glossed over if asked, but this is long already.
